note: Report prepared on 6 August 2026. The analysis covered the websites of movements (Evrópuhreyfingin, SJÁ, Heimssýn, Áfram Ísland, Til vinstri við ESB, Frjálst land), media outlets (Vísir, mbl.is, RÚV, DV, Heimildin, Viðskiptablaðið, Bændablaðið, Skessuhorn, Austurfrétt, Feykir, BB.is, Eyjafréttir, Vikublaðið, Útvarp Saga, Mannlíf, Nútíminn), as well as open discussion on Reddit and Facebook. Neutral news reports are not counted in the columns.
mv.ja.0.description: The main pro-European organisation, chaired by Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon; runs the YES side’s campaign headquarters.
mv.ja.1.description: A cross-party grassroots movement founded in June 2026; wants the nation to vote yes in order to see the accession treaty.
mv.ja.2.description: A youth movement of pro-Europeans working against disinformation in the run-up to the vote.
arg.vextir.title: Lower interest rates and a stable currency
arg.vextir.text: The euro would lower interest rates for households and businesses (even from ~9% to ~3%), eliminate indexation and the króna risk premium, and create economic stability that the króna has never achieved.
arg.kikja.title: A vote on talks — let’s see the agreement
arg.kikja.text: The vote is only about continuing negotiations, not membership. The nation would receive a finished agreement in hand and have the final say in a second vote — there is nothing to lose by taking a look.
arg.ahrif.title: A seat at the table instead of EEA powerlessness
arg.ahrif.text: Iceland currently implements a large share of EU rules through the EEA without any voting rights. Full membership provides a seat in the Council of Ministers, the Commission and Parliament — small states carry relatively significant weight.
arg.kjor.title: Lower prices and better living standards
arg.kjor.text: Membership would lower food prices (figures from 3% up to 25–30% have been cited), increase competition in banking and insurance services, and bring consumers European consumer protection.
arg.hraedslu.title: A response to fearmongering
arg.hraedslu.text: Claims about a European army, seizure of resources and loss of sovereignty are described as fearmongering; dire predictions about the EEA, EFTA and NATO never came true.
arg.serlausnir.title: Special arrangements are realistic — the quota remains Icelandic
arg.serlausnir.text: Catch history determines quota allocation, so it would remain Icelandic; all new member states have obtained special arrangements, and Iceland is in a strong negotiating position.
arg.oryggi.title: Security and shelter in uncertain times
arg.oryggi.text: In a world of tariff wars, economic sanctions and military threats, a small state needs shelter in a strong alliance; the EU protects its member states against external pressure.
arg.gildi.title: Shared European values
arg.gildi.text: Membership means solidarity around peace, democracy, human rights and the rule of law with Europe’s democracies at a time of growing authoritarian forces.
arg.lydraedi.title: Let the nation decide
arg.lydraedi.text: A referendum on such a major issue strengthens democracy; voters have the right to take a position and have the final say on the agreement.
arg.byggd.title: Regional funds for rural Iceland
arg.byggd.text: EU regional development and cohesion funds would finance roads, bridges, tunnels and infrastructure in rural areas.
arg.taekifaeri.title: Opportunities for young people
arg.taekifaeri.text: Education, jobs and home purchases at affordable interest rates in 27 countries; high interest rates hit young people hardest.
mv.nei.0.description: A cross-party movement of sovereigntists on European issues; runs the campaign “Afþökkum aðild að ESB”.
mv.nei.1.description: A broad NO coalition founded in July 2026, led among others by Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson and Björn Zoëga.
mv.nei.2.description: A left-wing organisation against EU membership, marketisation and militarisation.
arg.fullveldi.title: Transfer of sovereignty
arg.fullveldi.text: Membership would transfer legislative and judicial authority to EU institutions; such a transfer would not comply with the Constitution without amendments and runs counter to the sovereignty established in 1918.
arg.sjavarutvegur.title: Control over fisheries to Brussels
arg.sjavarutvegur.text: The EU’s Common Fisheries Policy would hold undivided authority over fishery resources; the experience of Ireland and Malta shows that small nations come out second best.
arg.spurning.title: The question is misleading
arg.spurning.text: The vote is in reality about an application for membership, not “talks” — the EU only accepts applications for full membership, and it is not possible to resume talks that broke off a decade ago.
arg.adlogun.title: Talks are adaptation, not exploration
arg.adlogun.text: It is not possible to “just take a look”: the application process entails adapting legislation and public administration to the EU as it proceeds, and it is difficult to turn back once the process has begun.
arg.ees.title: The EEA serves Iceland well
arg.ees.text: The EEA Agreement already guarantees market access and protects interests and sovereignty better than membership; Iceland retains an independent trade policy outside the customs union.
arg.efnahagur.title: Iceland fares better outside the EU
arg.efnahagur.text: Economic growth, employment, productivity and purchasing power are higher in Iceland than in most EU states; the EU is grappling with debt, an energy crisis and declining competitiveness.
arg.umbod.title: No mandate — broken promises
arg.umbod.text: There is no electoral mandate for reviving the application; politicians promised that the EU would not be a priority issue, and a democratic deficit characterises both the process and the Union itself.
arg.undanthagur.title: No permanent exemptions
arg.undanthagur.text: No country has received a permanent exemption from the EU’s fisheries or agricultural policy; special arrangements are temporary and subject to the power of the Commission.
arg.evra.title: The euro is not a magic solution
arg.evra.text: Growth in the euro area is far lower than in Iceland; Finland, with the euro, has the weakest growth in the Nordic region, and the cost of the euro is lower growth and higher unemployment.
arg.hervaeding.title: Militarisation of the EU
arg.hervaeding.text: The EU is integrating foreign and military policy and demanding increased military spending; Iceland should remain a country without armed forces and a voice for peace outside the military alliances of great powers.
arg.ahrifaleysi.title: The vanishing weight of a small state
arg.ahrifaleysi.text: Iceland would get about 6 seats out of 720 and ~0.08% voting weight in the Council; remote power in Brussels would be even more distant to rural communities than power in Reykjavík already is.
arg.kostnadur.title: High direct cost
arg.kostnadur.text: Membership would cost around ISK 30 billion a year in contributions, the talks themselves around ISK 2 billion, and EU climate rules have already cost Iceland tens of billions.
arg.oafturkraeft.title: Leaving is nearly impossible
arg.oafturkraeft.text: The experience of Brexit shows that leaving the EU is enormously difficult and costly; for a small state, membership is in practice an irreversible commitment.
arg.landbunadur.title: Agriculture at risk
arg.landbunadur.text: Tariff protection would disappear and domestic food production, especially dairy production, would not withstand competition; promises of lower prices for consumers are greatly exaggerated.
arg.nagrannar.title: No neighbouring country is in the EU
arg.nagrannar.text: Norway, Switzerland, Greenland and the Faroe Islands are all outside the EU and doing well; Iceland has more in common with them than with the continent.
art.0.title: Accession talks are negotiations
art.0.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs explains that the vote concerns only whether to begin negotiations, not membership, and that the nation will have the final say on a completed agreement.
art.1.title: What Iceland will fight for in negotiations with the EU
art.1.summary: The Executive Director of the Samfylkingin parliamentary group responds to criticism about unclear negotiating objectives and sets out Iceland’s red lines on fishing grounds, water and energy.
art.2.title: Iceland 2.0
art.2.summary: The chair of Evrópuhreyfingin presents three main arguments for membership: infrastructure development through regional funds, the euro, and security in a multinational alliance.
art.3.title: Should we let ourselves be deceived? The opportunities for rural communities
art.3.summary: Rural communities would benefit in particular from EU membership through regional and cohesion funds and larger markets, contrary to the scaremongering of the NO side.
art.4.title: The implementation deception
art.4.summary: Iceland adopts 75–80% of the EU’s internal market rules without any influence; the current EEA status is said to be unacceptable for a sovereign state, while membership would provide real power.
art.5.title: Three groups that would benefit most from Iceland joining the EU
art.5.summary: Businesses, indebted households, and rural communities would benefit most: predictability, lower interest rates, a tariff-free market, and regional development funds.
art.6.title: Marco Rubio’s call for a stronger Europe — what does it mean for Iceland?
art.6.summary: The United States’ demand for a stronger Europe and a changed security environment strengthen the case for Iceland to complete accession talks and secure shelter.
art.7.title: The influence of Icelanders could equal that of 15 million Germans
art.7.summary: A board member of SJÁ calculates, using the Banzhaf method, that each Icelander’s voting power in the EU Council of Ministers would be about 37 times that of each German — today that power is zero.
art.8.title: Can we do better for Icelandic households?
art.8.summary: The managing director of SJÁ asks why Icelanders accept high interest rates and inflation that European households do not know; let us see the agreement first.
art.9.title: Pawel Bartoszek: The talks are about an agreement — information — not membership!
art.9.summary: The chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee says the no movement misleadingly equates talks with membership; Sweden, Finland, and Malta secured special terms.
art.10.title: Why did we set out on this journey?
art.10.summary: A former foreign minister traces Iceland’s European path from EFTA in 1970 and says accession talks are the logical continuation; an isolated island nation needs allies.
art.11.title: The heart of the matter
art.11.summary: The debate gets stuck in semantic quibbling instead of the substance: the nation votes on talks and later again on the agreement itself — a double democratic process.
art.12.title: The jack, the spare tire, and the opportunities
art.12.summary: An analogy about a flat tire illustrates Icelanders’ interest-rate problem; the euro is said to be the only realistic tool for bringing rates down after a century of krona instability.
art.13.title: Does size matter?
art.13.summary: It rebuts concerns about the powerlessness of small states: small nations have proportionally greater representation and the highest satisfaction with membership (Ireland 93%); Brexit shows the alternative.
art.14.title: Don’t say NO… say maybe
art.14.summary: The vote is about continuing talks, not membership; the best living standards in the world are in EU countries, and there is nothing to lose by examining the agreement.
art.15.title: We could get a good agreement
art.15.summary: Iceland is in a strong negotiating position: fishing rights are based on historical use, so the quota would remain Icelandic, the krona premium would disappear, and regional development funds would open up.
art.16.title: Here is a fact: there is no such thing as a European army
art.16.summary: It rebuts claims that membership would force Iceland into a European army; military affairs remain under each state’s control, and Iceland’s lack of armed forces would be respected.
art.17.title: No is bigger than Yes
art.17.summary: No is said to be the more consequential choice than yes because it closes the door for generations: interest rates could go from ~9% to ~3% and food prices fall by 25–30%.
art.18.title: The election of young people
art.18.summary: The vote concerns above all the future of young people: mortgage interest rates, study and job opportunities in 27 countries, and stability.
art.19.title: … and I want the nation to have its say
art.19.summary: Direct democracy on such a major issue strengthens democracy; voters have the right to take a position between parliamentary elections.
art.20.title: Is this acceptable for a sovereign nation?
art.20.summary: EEA states have almost no formal influence over EU legislation; Iceland accepts rules without voting rights, and that fits poorly with sovereignty.
art.21.title: Let’s be positive in August
art.21.summary: An encouragement to vote yes on 29 August: a strong negotiating position in a changed world, all new member states received special arrangements, and the nation gets direct involvement in the process.
art.22.title: Dihydrogen monoxide
art.22.summary: The dihydrogen monoxide analogy shows how fearmongering distorts the debate: ordinary international trade becomes an “overthrow of resources.”
art.23.title: YES means yes to new opportunities
art.23.summary: Yes ensures lower interest rates, stability, and better access to education and research; high interest rates hit young people hardest.
art.24.title: Disorder on the conscience
art.24.summary: The NO side is deliberately muddying the debate; the Venice Commission confirms that the vote is on negotiations, not membership.
art.25.title: YES to SEE
art.25.summary: Article marking the founding meeting of SJÁ at Kjarvalsstaðir with over 300 founding members; yes means the nation gets to see the agreement and make an informed decision.
art.26.title: Fearmongering against accession talks
art.26.summary: Fearmongering characterizes the arguments against negotiations; earlier dire predictions about NATO, EFTA and the EEA proved false, and it is better to see the agreement first.
art.27.title: The vote is a pivotal moment
art.27.summary: The EEA is a temporary solution without democratic participation, and the króna costs around 300 billion annually; the negotiations should be completed and a vote held on a finished agreement.
art.28.title: EU - Monster or shelter
art.28.summary: The dire predictions about the EEA never came true; the EU’s main opponents in the world are Pútín and Trump, and the Union is a shelter for a small nation against geopolitical threats.
art.29.title: Iceland and the new job
art.29.summary: Compares EU membership to a job offer with better terms that Iceland is hesitating to consider; there is no risk in exploring the opportunity.
art.30.title: The Elite’s guest list
art.30.summary: The business elite’s opposition to the EU is based on self-interest in an unstable króna economy; lower interest rates and stability benefit ordinary people.
art.31.title: Let’s look inside the package!
art.31.summary: Compares an accession agreement to a Christmas present that should be opened: the nation should get the facts straight before a final decision is made.
art.32.title: Old news and new
art.32.summary: Opponents of membership rely on an outdated image of Europe; the facts show a continent thriving in innovation, the economy and defense.
art.33.title: Let us stand guard over our values and ideals
art.33.summary: Iceland should join the EU to defend freedom, peace, human rights and democracy at a time of growing authoritarian forces, in solidarity with Ukraine.
art.34.title: When international trade is weaponized
art.34.summary: Tariff wars and economic sanctions have become political weapons; a small state dependent on international trade needs shelter in a trade alliance.
art.35.title: Europe will not yield to Trump’s threats over Greenland
art.35.summary: The EU responds to threats by deepening free-trade ties around the world; solidarity against external threats protects small states.
art.36.title: Let’s be YES-positive in August
art.36.summary: Iceland has not achieved price stability in seven decades; young people need a real currency, and the nation can reject an agreement later.
art.37.title: Adjustment, what adjustment?
art.37.summary: Rejects claims of irreversible adjustment: no legal changes were made during the 2009–2013 negotiations, and there will be no systemic changes without a second vote.
art.38.title: We don’t need the EU – or do we?
art.38.summary: Resources alone do not explain high interest rates; small nations like Ireland and Malta benefit from the EU, and there is no risk in seeing the terms of an agreement first.
art.39.title: I am not a Europhile
art.39.summary: Support for negotiations is based on interests, not love of Europe: the króna ties up 1.000 billion in foreign exchange reserves and costs over 100 billion annually in interest.
art.40.title: Remarkable hypocrisy
art.40.summary: Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn is being hypocritical in its response to the Venice Commission’s opinion that the vote concerns the continuation of negotiations, not membership.
art.41.title: “Slava Ukraini” - Does Iceland share Ukraine’s path?
art.41.summary: Ukraine’s European struggle is compared with Iceland’s position; the EU strengthens small nations and protects their languages and culture rather than weakening them.
art.42.title: This is not a U-turn – it is facing the future
art.42.summary: Negotiations with the EU are a natural continuation of Iceland’s European cooperation, as it is already in the EEA and Schengen without full influence; sovereignty lies in informed choice.
art.43.title: Is it better to know than to assume?
art.43.summary: A yes vote makes it possible to complete the negotiations so the nation can make a final decision with a finished agreement in hand instead of relying on speculation.
art.44.title: The European Union, more than a customs union
art.44.summary: The EU is much more than an economic union: human rights, consumer protection, workers’ rights, environmental issues, and solidarity funds.
art.45.title: Helga Vala criticizes “politics of fear” in the debate on EU accession talks
art.45.summary: Sovereignty consists precisely in the right to enter into international agreements; fearmongering distorts the debate, and the nation will have the final say in any case.
art.46.title: Europe: Open market or closed state?
art.46.summary: The EU has evolved from a customs union into a centrally governed federal state; membership would cost control over fisheries, independent trade agreements, and around 30 billion annually.
art.47.title: Ólafur Ragnar presents strong arguments against EU membership
art.47.summary: The former president sets out economic and geographical arguments against membership: no neighboring country is in the EU, and Iceland, Norway, and Switzerland are growing faster than the EU states.
art.48.title: Continuation or new accession talks?
art.48.summary: The former Speaker of Alþingi considers the question fundamentally misleading: it conflates the continuation of old talks with entirely new accession negotiations.
art.49.title: Transfer of a nation’s sovereignty
art.49.summary: Former Supreme Court justice: membership would entail a major transfer of sovereignty, especially legislative power, which would not comply with the constitution without amendments.
art.50.title: Growth is lower in the euro area
art.50.summary: Vice Chairman of Framsókn: growth in the euro area is 1% compared with 2.5% in Iceland; the opportunity cost of the euro is lower growth and higher unemployment.
art.51.title: Áfram Ísland launches website and publishes new report
art.51.summary: A new report by Áfram Ísland compares living standards: Iceland outperforms EU states in growth, employment, productivity, purchasing power, and public finances.
art.52.title: Áfram Ísland!
art.52.summary: Former minister: the vote is about Icelanders’ control over their own destiny; membership would cost control over fisheries, agriculture, and the currency.
art.53.title: No, Ingibjörg Sólrún, this is the heart of the matter
art.53.summary: Chairman of Heimssýn: the heart of the matter is surrendering sovereignty — no one applies for membership unless they want to join, the cost is over 100 billion annually, and withdrawal is virtually impossible.
art.54.title: Iceland and the EU – special status and accession talks
art.54.summary: A former ambassador points to the incompatibility between Iceland’s non-negotiable demands for control over resources and the EU’s fundamental rules on integration.
art.55.title: Foreign Minister’s referendum proposal gets a failing grade
art.55.summary: Less than a quarter of the comments supported the proposal unchanged; Carl Baudenbacher considered the question misleading because it is not possible to “continue” talks that were broken off a decade ago.
art.56.title: The book about the EU
art.56.summary: Frosti’s book on “what’s in the package”: democratic deficit, aging populations, unfunded pension systems, debt, and high energy costs within the EU.
art.57.title: A fundamental difference between the EEA and the EU
art.57.summary: The difference between the EEA and the EU is one of kind, not degree: membership places the Court of Justice of the EU above Icelandic law and entails a transfer of legislative and judicial power.
art.58.title: So was it permissible to deceive, after all?
art.58.summary: Criticism of Kristrún Frostadóttir for a policy reversal: before the election it was “forbidden to deceive,” but now the EU issue is being pushed forward without broad consensus.
art.59.title: Áfram Ísland
art.59.summary: Founding meeting of Áfram Ísland: Iceland is a land of opportunity outside the EU, and the future should be decided on Icelanders’ own terms.
art.60.title: Protocol 35 to the EEA Agreement and the Constitution
art.60.summary: Law professor: the precedence rule of EEA law under Protocol 35 may conflict with the Constitution because it creates “super-laws” across broad areas.
art.61.title: Iceland and the EU – wishful thinking and facts
art.61.summary: A comparison of the promises made during the 2009–2013 talks with the legal reality: permanent exemptions in fisheries were never on offer.
art.62.title: What’s in the package?
art.62.summary: Membership would mean Brussels controlling fisheries and energy policy, only 6 parliamentary seats out of 720, and a weaker special position for Iceland in security matters.
art.63.title: An application requires a decision – not a call
art.63.summary: The old membership application does not continue on its own; there is no electoral mandate for the process, and special arrangements are not legally permanent.
art.64.title: Categorically rejects any further steps toward the EU
art.64.summary: The chair of Heimssýn rejects any further steps toward EU membership; Iceland’s interests are best served outside the Union.
art.65.title: Is it fear to say no?
art.65.summary: A no vote is not fear but a critical assessment: the process would take 3–4 years, tie up the public administration, and freeze other free trade agreements.
art.66.title: Let’s say NO for future generations
art.66.summary: EU membership is an almost irreversible commitment for a small state, as Brexit has shown.
art.67.title: Why must no not be said?
art.67.summary: No is a legitimate democratic position that is wrongly dismissed as hostility to information; accession talks are not a neutral process.
art.68.title: Learn from history: Say NO to the EU!
art.68.summary: History shows that the United States has served Iceland better than the European states; sovereignty is at risk vis-à-vis Brussels.
art.69.title: The talks are about alignment
art.69.summary: The EU’s own documents show that the talks are about aligning the applicant state with the Union’s regulatory framework before any agreement would be put to a vote.
art.70.title: Whether to begin accession to the EU
art.70.summary: The vote is in fact about whether to begin accession to the EU, since alignment takes place within the negotiation process itself.
art.71.title: The EU Package
art.71.summary: The talks would cost around 2 billion and the referendum 600–700 million; the militarisation of the EU and the adoption of its foreign policy are causes for concern.
art.72.title: The referendum is about Iceland’s membership of the European Union
art.72.summary: Opinion piece in Viðskiptablaðið: the vote is in reality about Iceland’s EU membership, not only about talks.
art.73.title: They do not want to talk about the European Union at all
art.73.summary: Submitted article in Morgunblaðið: the yes side avoids discussing the European Union itself, even though membership is the ultimate goal of the talks.
art.74.title: Why are EU talks unwise at this point in time?
art.74.summary: Talks are unwise now because of weaknesses within the EU (the Draghi report, political instability) and the risk that investment in fisheries and energy would freeze.
art.75.title: Referendum on EU talks said to be possible as early as August
art.75.summary: Criticism of the speed of the process: Iceland could join the EU faster than any other applicant country if yes prevails.
art.76.title: The organisation Til Vinstri við ESB founded
art.76.summary: A left-wing organisation against EU membership: the free movement of capital increases inequality and there is a risk that Icelanders will be drawn into the EU’s militarisation.
art.77.title: Press release – founding of Til vinstri við ESB
art.77.summary: The EEA has become one-sided, marketisation is intensifying, and militarisation threatens Iceland’s role for peace; Iceland should be an advocate for peace outside the EU.
art.78.title: The policy statement and a reminder
art.78.summary: Iceland should reject EU centralisation and choose international cooperation on its own terms in the interests of peace, democracy, and humanity.
art.79.title: Newsletter #4 – Meeting on fisheries issues
art.79.summary: The EU grants only transitional periods, but no permanent exemptions in fisheries, as Malta’s experience shows; Norway has repeatedly rejected membership.
art.80.title: Militarisation and the EU
art.80.summary: The EU is unifying its foreign and military policy; Iceland should remain a demilitarised country for the foreseeable future and stand with small nations.
art.81.title: Iceland does not belong in the EU Emissions Trading System
art.81.summary: Participation in the EU Emissions Trading System cost Iceland 144 billion in 2017–2024; the country is already a leader in clean energy and has no business being in the system.
art.82.title: Nothing about the negotiating objectives
art.82.summary: Managing director of Bændasamtökin: the parliamentary resolution contains no negotiating objectives, and without an analysis of interests the nation cannot take an informed position.
art.83.title: The issue is about the right to govern
art.83.summary: With membership, control over fishery resources would shift to Brussels, where Iceland’s weight would be about 0.08%; Ireland’s experience is a warning.
art.84.title: The injustice of Reykjavík or of the EU?
art.84.summary: Neglect of East Iceland by the central authorities in the capital is linked to even more distant power in Brussels; ETS rules raise production costs in rural areas.
art.85.title: “Irresponsible claims being made about agriculture and food prices”
art.85.summary: A dairy farmer warns that milk production will run into trouble without tariff protection; doubts that food prices will fall significantly for consumers.
art.86.title: The EU accepts applications for membership — not for talks
art.86.summary: In 2009, Iceland formally applied for full membership under Article 49 of the Treaty; talk of “just talks” is misleading.
art.87.title: Agriculture and the EU: Special arrangements are not exemptions
art.87.summary: There are no examples of permanent exemptions from the EU’s agricultural policy; the Finns’ northern support was built into the regulatory framework, not an exemption.
art.88.title: Misleading comparison with the Norwegians
art.88.summary: The foreign minister’s comparison with Norway’s 1994 talks does not hold up: the EU adaptation process came later, and new talks would entail adaptation.
art.89.title: Information chaos from the chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee
art.89.summary: Claims of up to a 25% drop in food prices do not stand up: the actual decrease is closer to 3%, and many products are already duty-free.
art.90.title: Says MPs speak differently in Eyjar than in Reykjavík
art.90.summary: The chairman of Ísfélagið wants to postpone the vote while inflation remains high; the fisheries sector needs stability, and Iceland is not ready for the euro.
art.91.title: Referendum on talks with the EU — Why, and why now?
art.91.summary: The Progressive Party parliamentary group chair: a new vote would concern the start of new talks, not the continuation of old ones, since the EU has changed dramatically; Iceland is doing well in the EEA.
art.92.title: Sovereignty, informed debate, and a responsible decision
art.92.summary: The vote is about sovereignty: control over fisheries and energy should remain domestic, EU centralisation is increasing, and there are no negotiating objectives.
art.93.title: The government must be candid on the European Union issue — Examining agriculture
art.93.summary: A former minister demands clear answers on fisheries and agriculture; the agriculture chapter was never opened in 2009–2013, and temporary exemptions are not enough.
art.94.title: The referendum entails a mandate for adaptation to the EU
art.94.summary: Young against the EU: a yes vote entails a mandate for an extensive process of adapting to EU rules, and it will be difficult to turn back.
art.95.title: The EU referendum could cause a political crisis
art.95.summary: A narrow victory or low turnout weakens the authorities’ mandate, and the advisory nature of the vote invites disputes over interpretation.
art.96.title: Misleading information about the EU vote on the National Electoral Commission website
art.96.summary: Promotional material from the National Electoral Commission conceals that a yes vote means a formal membership application process, not simple talks.
art.97.title: Ólafur Ragnar: “The real-world examples simply do not fit this ideology about the EU”
art.97.summary: The EU debate is ideological froth rather than facts: Iceland recovered from the crash faster than EU states, and no Nordic neighbouring country uses the euro except Finland.
art.98.title: EU parliamentarian says the Union itself is trying to influence elections
art.98.summary: MEP Fidias Panayiotou accuses the EU itself of trying to influence elections in other countries; doubts raised about the Union’s love of democracy.
art.99.title: Some of the lies, nonsense, and deceptions coming from Heimssýn regarding the EU
art.99.summary: A summary of claims by the chair of Heimssýn that the author says are misrepresentations which the media let pass unchallenged.
art.100.title: It emerges that economic growth is lower in Iceland than in the EU and unemployment is similar
art.100.summary: Data presented showing that economic growth in Iceland (0.9%) is lower than in the EU (1.4%) and has been virtually zero per capita since 2018 — a direct response to the NO side’s economic arguments.
art.101.title: Anti-EU leaflets distributed everywhere in Mathöll
art.101.summary: A user describes dissatisfaction with the aggressive leaflet propaganda of the NO side and says they intend to vote YES, partly as a protest.
art.102.title: Chair of Heimssýn warns of violence if Iceland joins the EU
art.102.summary: Remarks by Haraldur Ólafsson about possible violence are condemned in a thread that is highly critical of the NO side.
art.103.title: (Yet another) EU reflection
art.103.summary: Money flows from vested interests into propaganda against the EU show who benefits from the status quo; the public interest would be better served within the EU.
art.104.title: Permanent exemptions were part of the EU from the outset
art.104.summary: News sharing: permanent opt-outs and special arrangements have always existed within the EU, supporting the YES side’s argument that Iceland has room to negotiate.
art.105.title: EU willing to discuss exemptions from fisheries legislation with Icelanders
art.105.summary: Report that the EU is prepared to discuss exemptions on fisheries issues; undermines the NO side’s biggest counterargument.
art.106.title: The EU, or not?
art.106.summary: Why don’t opponents simply say yes to talks to see an actual agreement — the nation can always reject membership later?
art.107.title: Why are Sjálfstæðismenn and Miðflokksmenn so afraid of the EU?
