detail.vextir.0: According to the YES side, a stable currency is the main economic argument for membership. It argues that the euro would lower interest rates for households and businesses, potentially from around 9% to around 3%, eliminate indexation and the so-called króna premium. In its view, membership would thus create the economic stability that the króna has never achieved.
detail.vextir.1: In an article on the Evrópuhreyfingin website, Dóra Magnúsdóttir compares Icelanders’ interest-rate problem to a flat tyre and says the euro is the only realistic tool for bringing rates down after a century of króna instability. Óðinn Freyr Baldursson writes on visir.is that the króna ties up 1.000 billion in foreign exchange reserves and costs over 100 billion annually in interest, while Björgvin G. Sigurðsson says in an article on dv.is that the króna costs about 300 billion annually. Thomas Möller claims that interest rates could fall from around 9% to around 3% and that the króna premium would disappear with membership.
detail.vextir.2: Berglind Guðmundsdóttir, managing director of SJÁ, asks in an article on Vísir why Icelanders accept high interest rates and inflation that European households do not know. Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon, chair of Evrópuhreyfingin, believes indebted households are among the groups that would benefit most from membership because of lower interest rates and greater predictability. Óðinn Freyr Baldursson also argues that the business elite’s opposition to the EU is based on self-interest in an unstable króna economy, whereas lower interest rates and stability would benefit ordinary people.
detail.kikja.0: The YES side emphasises that the vote concerns only whether to continue the talks, not membership itself. It says the nation will receive a completed agreement in hand and have the final say in a second vote. Therefore, there is nothing to lose by examining the agreement.
detail.kikja.1: In an article on visir.is, Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir explains that the vote concerns only whether to begin negotiations, not membership, and that the nation will have the final say on a completed agreement. Pawel Bartoszek, chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee, says on dv.is that the NO movement misleadingly equates talks with membership, and Ingibjörg Sólrún Gísladóttir describes the process as a two-stage democratic process: the nation votes on talks and later votes again on the agreement itself. Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson points out that the Venice Commission confirms that the vote is on talks, not membership.
detail.kikja.2: On visir.is, Halldór Jörgen Olesen rejects the idea that talks entail irreversible adaptation; no legal changes were made during the 2009–2013 talks and no systemic changes will occur without a later vote. Berglind Guðmundsdóttir, managing director of SJÁ, says that a yes means the nation gets to see the agreement and make an informed decision. Óli Rúnar Ástþórsson writes in Feykir that a yes vote would make it possible to conclude the talks so that the nation can make a final decision with a completed agreement in hand instead of speculation.
detail.ahrif.0: The YES side points out that Iceland already implements a large share of EU rules through the EEA Agreement without any voting rights. In its view, full membership would give Iceland a seat in the Council of Ministers, the Commission, and Parliament. It also argues that small states have proportionally significant influence within the Union.
detail.ahrif.1: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon writes on the Evrópuhreyfingin website that Iceland adopts 75–80% of EU internal market rules without any influence and that the current EEA status is unacceptable for a sovereign state. Kristján Vigfússon strikes the same note, saying that EEA states have almost no formal influence on EU legislation; Iceland accepts rules without voting rights, which fits poorly with sovereignty. Hjálmar Vilhjálmsson, a board member of SJÁ, calculates using the Banzhaf method that each Icelander’s voting weight in the EU Council of Ministers would be about 37 times that of each German — today that weight is zero.
detail.ahrif.2: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson rejects concerns on the Evrópuhreyfingin website about the powerlessness of small states and says small nations have proportionally more representatives and the highest satisfaction with membership, with Ireland at 93%. In an article on dv.is, Björgvin G. Sigurðsson calls the EEA a temporary solution without democratic participation.
detail.kjor.0: According to the YES side, membership would lower food prices, with figures ranging from 3% up to 25–30% having been cited. It also says membership would increase competition in banking and insurance services and bring consumers European consumer protection.
detail.kjor.1: In articles on the Evrópuhreyfingin website, Thomas Möller claims that the best living standards in the world are found in EU countries and that food prices could fall by 25–30%. Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon says that businesses, indebted households, and rural areas would benefit most from membership, among other things because of a tariff-free market and predictability. Steinar Harðarson writes in Eyjafréttir that the EU is much more than an economic union; it also encompasses consumer protection, workers’ rights, and human rights.
detail.kjor.2: On Reddit, the user Einn1Tveir2 has posted data showing that economic growth in Iceland (0.9%) is lower than in the EU (1.4%) and has been almost nonexistent per capita since 2018, presenting this as a direct response to the NO side’s economic arguments. Þorvaldur Ingi Jónsson writes on visir.is that natural resources alone do not explain high growth and that small nations such as Ireland and Malta benefit from the EU.
detail.hraedslu.0: The YES side says that claims about a European army, seizure of resources, and loss of sovereignty are fearmongering. It points out that dire predictions about the EEA, EFTA, and NATO never came true.
detail.hraedslu.1: Óðinn Freyr Baldursson rebuts, on the Evrópuhreyfingin website, claims that membership would force Iceland into a European army; military affairs would remain under each state’s control and Iceland’s non-military status would be respected. Guðfinna Jóh. Guðmundsdóttir writes on dv.is that fearmongering characterizes the case against talks and that earlier dire predictions about NATO, EFTA, and the EEA proved wrong. Helgi Hrafn Gunnarsson uses the dihydrogen monoxide analogy to show how alarmist language distorts the debate so that ordinary international trade becomes a “takeover of resources,” and Helga Vala Helgadóttir says in Mannlíf that sovereignty lies precisely in the right to make international agreements and that the nation would in any case have the final say.
detail.hraedslu.2: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson argues on visir.is that the NO side is deliberately confusing the debate. In public discussion on Reddit, the user Einn1Tveir2 has compiled claims by the chair of Heimssýn that he says are misrepresentations that the media let pass unchallenged, and in another thread Haraldur Ólafsson’s remarks about possible violence if Iceland joins the EU were condemned.
detail.serlausnir.0: The YES side argues that the quota would remain Icelandic because quota allocation is based on fishing history. It says that all new member states have obtained special arrangements and that Iceland is in a strong negotiating position.
detail.serlausnir.1: Pawel Bartoszek points out in an article on dv.is that Sweden, Finland, and Malta secured special terms. Thomas Möller writes on the Evrópuhreyfingin website that fishing rights are based on historical use, so the quota would remain Icelandic, and that all new member states have obtained special arrangements. Þórður Snær Júlíusson outlines Iceland’s red lines on fishing grounds, water, and energy on visir.is in response to criticism about unclear negotiating objectives.
detail.serlausnir.2: On Reddit, a news item has been shared saying that the EU is willing to discuss exemptions in fisheries matters, which is said to undermine the NO side’s biggest counterarguments. Another user points out that permanent exemptions and special arrangements have always existed within the EU, supporting the YES side’s argument about Iceland’s negotiating possibilities.
detail.oryggi.0: The YES side says that in a world of tariff wars, economic sanctions, and military threats, small states need shelter in a strong alliance. In its view, the EU protects its member states against external pressure.
detail.oryggi.1: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon, chair of Evrópuhreyfingin, cites security in a multinational alliance as one of his three main arguments for membership and believes that the United States’ demand for a stronger Europe and the changed security environment strengthen the case for Iceland to complete accession talks and secure shelter. Ingibjörg Sólrún Gísladóttir writes on dv.is that an isolated island nation needs allies and that accession talks are the logical continuation of Iceland’s European path since EFTA in 1970.
detail.oryggi.2: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson says on the Evrópuhreyfingin website that tariff wars and economic sanctions have become political weapons and that small states dependent on international trade need shelter in a trade alliance. Kristján Vigfússon points out that the EU responds to external threats by deepening free-trade relationships around the world and that solidarity protects small states. Vésteinn Ólason writes in Heimildin that the union is a small nation’s shelter against geopolitical threats; the EU’s main opponents in the world are Putin and Trump.
detail.gildi.0: In the YES side’s view, membership means solidarity for peace, democracy, human rights, and the rule of law with Europe’s democracies. It says this matters at a time of growing authoritarian forces.
detail.gildi.1: Bjarki F. Guðjónsson writes on the Evrópuhreyfingin website that Iceland should join the EU to defend freedom, peace, human rights, and democracy, in solidarity with Ukraine. Jóhannes Finnur Halldórsson compares Ukraine’s struggle for Europe in Skessuhorn with Iceland’s position and says the EU strengthens small nations and protects their language and culture rather than weakening them.
detail.gildi.2: Steinar Harðarson writes in Eyjafréttir that the EU is much more than an economic alliance: it combines human rights, consumer protection, workers’ rights, environmental issues, and solidarity funds. Thomas Möller argues that opponents of membership rely on an outdated image of Europe; the facts show a continent flourishing in innovation, the economy, and defence.
detail.lydraedi.0: The YES side says that a referendum on such a major issue strengthens democracy. Voters have the right to take a position and have the final say on an agreement.
detail.lydraedi.1: Helga Vala Helgadóttir writes on the Evrópuhreyfingin website that direct democracy on such a major issue strengthens democracy and that voters have the right to take a position between parliamentary elections. Ingibjörg Sólrún Gísladóttir describes the process on dv.is as a double democratic process: the nation votes on talks and later votes again on the agreement itself.
detail.lydraedi.2: Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir emphasizes in an article on visir.is that the nation will have the final say on a completed agreement. Berglind Guðmundsdóttir, managing director of SJÁ, says that a yes means the nation gets to see the agreement and make an informed decision; SJÁ was founded at Kjarvalsstaðir with over 300 founding members.
detail.byggd.0: The YES side argues that the EU’s regional development and cohesion funds would particularly benefit rural Iceland. It says the funds would finance roads, bridges, tunnels, and other infrastructure in rural areas.
detail.byggd.1: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon, chair of Evrópuhreyfingin, cites infrastructure development through regional funds as one of his three main arguments for membership. In another article, he argues that rural Iceland would especially benefit from EU membership through regional and cohesion funds and larger markets, contrary to what he calls NO-side fearmongering. He also considers rural Iceland one of the three groups that would benefit most from membership, alongside businesses and indebted households.
detail.byggd.2: Thomas Möller writes on the Evrópuhreyfingin website that membership would open regional funds to Iceland, alongside the disappearance of the krona risk premium. In his view, Iceland is in a strong negotiating position in such talks.
detail.taekifaeri.0: The YES side says that membership would open opportunities for young people to study, work, and buy housing at affordable interest rates in 27 countries. It points out that high interest rates hit young people hardest.
detail.taekifaeri.1: Thomas Möller writes on the Evrópuhreyfingin website that the vote is above all about the future of young people: mortgage interest rates, study and work opportunities in 27 countries, and stability. In another article, he says that a yes would secure lower interest rates, stability, and better access to education and research, and reiterates that high interest rates hit young people hardest.
detail.fullveldi.0: The NO side argues that EU membership would transfer legislative and judicial power from Iceland to the union’s institutions. In its view, such a transfer would not be compatible with the Icelandic constitution without amending it. It also says that the transfer would run counter to the sovereignty Iceland gained in 1918.
detail.fullveldi.1: Jón Steinar Gunnlaugsson, former Supreme Court judge, writes on the Heimssýn website that membership would involve a sweeping transfer of sovereignty, especially legislative power, that would not comply with the constitution without amendments. Law professor Stefán Már Stefánsson argues in an article for Heimssýn that the primacy of EEA law under Protocol 35 may conflict with the constitution because it creates “super-laws” in broad areas. Erna Bjarnadóttir says at Heimssýn that the difference between the EEA and the EU is one of kind, not degree: membership would place the Court of Justice of the EU above Icelandic law.
detail.fullveldi.2: Björn Bjarnason, former minister, says the vote is about Icelanders’ control over their own destiny and that membership would cost them control over fisheries, agriculture, and currency. Ingibjörg Isaksen, parliamentary group chair of Framsóknarflokkurinn, writes in Vikublaðið that the vote is about sovereignty and that control over fisheries and energy should remain domestic. A Reddit thread also expresses astonishment at the silence of Icelandic media about the EU’s Chat Control surveillance plans and presents privacy arguments against membership.
detail.sjavarutvegur.0: The NO side says that the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy would hold exclusive power over the fishery resource if Iceland joined the union. It points to the experience of Ireland and Malta, which it says shows that small nations lose out in this system.
detail.sjavarutvegur.1: Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson writes in Skessuhorn that with membership, control over marine resources would shift to Brussels, where Iceland’s weight would be about 0.08%, and says Ireland’s experience is a warning. Hannes Hólmsteinn Gissurarson argues on the Heimssýn website that membership would cost control over fisheries and independent trade agreements. Hreinn Loftsson says in an article for Heimssýn that membership would mean Brussels controlling fisheries and energy policy.
detail.sjavarutvegur.2: Albert Jónsson, former ambassador, points to what he sees as an incompatibility between Iceland’s non-negotiable demands for control over resources and the EU’s fundamental rules on integration. Ögmundur Jónasson, former minister, demands clear answers in Vikublaðið on fisheries and agriculture and notes that the agriculture chapter was never opened in the 2009–2013 talks. Einar Sigurðsson, chair of Ísfélagið, says in Eyjafréttir that the fisheries sector needs stability and wants the vote postponed while inflation is high.
detail.spurning.0: The NO side argues that the ballot question is misleading: in reality, the vote is on an accession application, not “talks.” The EU only accepts applications for full membership, and talks that broke off a decade ago cannot simply be resumed.
detail.spurning.1: Birgir Ármannsson, former Speaker of Alþingi, considers the question fundamentally misleading because it conflates the continuation of old talks with entirely new accession talks. The Heimssýn website states that fewer than a quarter of consultation responses supported the foreign minister’s proposal unchanged and that Carl Baudenbacher considered the question misleading because it is not possible to “continue” talks that broke off a decade ago. Erna Bjarnadóttir writes in Feykir that in 2009 Iceland formally applied for full membership under Article 49 of the treaty and that talk of “just talks” is misleading.
detail.spurning.2: An opinion piece in Viðskiptablaðið says that the vote is in reality about Iceland’s membership of the EU rather than only about talks, and a submitted article in Morgunblaðið argues that the YES side avoids discussing the European Union itself even though membership is the talks’ ultimate objective. Júlíus Valsson writes at Útvarp Saga that the National Electoral Commission’s informational material conceals that a yes vote means a formal accession process. Hildur Sverrisdóttir, parliamentary group chair of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn, says the question is misleading and the talks are a waste of time and money.
detail.adlogun.0: The NO side says it is not possible to “peek inside the package”: the application process involves the ongoing adaptation of Icelandic legislation and administration to the EU. It is difficult to turn back once the process has begun.
detail.adlogun.1: Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson argues in an article on Vísir that the EU’s own documents show that the talks are about adapting an applicant country to the union’s regulatory framework before any vote on an agreement. In another article, he says the referendum is really about whether to begin joining the EU, since the adaptation takes place in the negotiation process itself. On BB.is, he writes that the foreign minister’s comparison with Norway’s 1994 talks does not hold because the EU’s adaptation process came later.
detail.adlogun.2: Kjartan Magnússon of Ung gegn ESB says that a yes vote would amount to a mandate for an extensive adaptation process to the EU’s regulatory framework and that it will be difficult to turn back. Hnikarr Bjarmi Franklínsson writes on Vísir that the process would take 3–4 years, tie up the administration, and freeze other free-trade agreements. The pace of the process is also criticized on the Heimssýn website, which argues that Iceland could enter the EU faster than any other applicant country if yes prevails.
detail.ees.0: The NO side argues that the EEA Agreement already guarantees Iceland market access and protects its interests and sovereignty better than full membership would. Outside the customs union, Iceland also retains an independent trade policy.
detail.ees.1: Erna Bjarnadóttir writes at Heimssýn that the difference between the EEA and the EU is one of kind, not degree: membership would place the Court of Justice of the EU above Icelandic law and involve a transfer of legislative and judicial power. Hannes Hólmsteinn Gissurarson argues that the EU has evolved from a customs union into a centrally governed federal state and that membership would cost, among other things, independent trade agreements. Ingibjörg Isaksen says in Vikublaðið that Iceland is doing well in the EEA.
detail.ees.2: Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of Heimssýn, rejects any further steps toward EU membership and says Iceland’s interests are best served outside the union. The website Frjálst land claims that participation in the EU Emissions Trading System cost Iceland 144 billion in the years 2017–2024 and that the country has no business being in the system. Jökull Sólberg of Til vinstri við ESB, on the other hand, says the EEA has become one-sided and that Iceland should be an advocate for peace outside the EU.
detail.efnahagur.0: The NO side says Iceland is better off outside the EU: growth, employment, productivity, and purchasing power are higher in Iceland than in most EU countries. At the same time, the EU is grappling with debt, an energy crisis, and declining competitiveness.
detail.efnahagur.1: A report by Áfram Ísland compares living standards and claims that Iceland outperforms EU countries in growth, employment, productivity, purchasing power, and public finances. Lilja Dögg Alfreðsdóttir, deputy chair of Framsóknarflokkurinn, says eurozone growth is 1% compared with 2.5% in Iceland. Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, former president, argues that Iceland, Norway, and Switzerland are growing faster than the EU countries and that Iceland recovered from the crash faster than they did.
detail.efnahagur.2: In his book, presented by Heimssýn, Frosti Sigurjónsson discusses the democratic deficit, ageing populations, unfunded pension systems, debt, and high energy costs within the EU. Kristinn Sv. Helgason writes in Heimildin that talks are unwise at this point because of the EU’s weaknesses, which he links in part to the Draghi report and political instability, and that there is a risk that investment in fisheries and energy will freeze.
detail.umbod.0: The NO side argues that there is no electoral mandate to revive the EU application. Politicians promised that the EU would not be a priority issue, and in its view a democratic deficit characterizes both the process and the union itself.
detail.umbod.1: On Heimssýn’s website, Kristrún Frostadóttir is criticised for a change of course: before the election it had been “forbidden to mislead,” but now the EU issue is being pushed forward without broad consensus. Erna Bjarnadóttir writes for Heimssýn that the old membership application does not continue automatically and that there is no electoral mandate for the process. Margrét Ágústa Sigurðardóttir, managing director of Bændasamtakanna, points out in Bændablaðið that the parliamentary resolution contains no negotiating objectives and that, without an analysis of the interests at stake, the nation cannot take an informed position.
detail.umbod.2: Páll Vilhjálmsson writes for Útvarp Saga that a narrow victory or low turnout would weaken the government’s mandate and that the advisory nature of the referendum opens the door to disputes over interpretation. Nútíminn quotes Member of the European Parliament Fidias Panayiotou as saying that the EU itself tries to influence elections in other countries. The NO side also believes, according to discussion on Reddit, that RÚV is biased in its coverage of the EU issue.
detail.undanthagur.0: The NO side says that no state has received a permanent exemption from the EU’s fisheries or agricultural policy. Special arrangements are temporary and subject to the authority of the European Commission.
detail.undanthagur.1: Hreinn Loftsson compares, on Heimssýn, the promises made during the 2009–2013 negotiations with the legal reality, and says that permanent exemptions in fisheries were never on offer. Erna Bjarnadóttir writes on BB.is that there are no examples of permanent exemptions from the EU’s agricultural policy; the Finns’ northern support was built into the regulatory framework rather than being an exemption. Ágúst Valves Jóhannesson of Til vinstri við ESB says that the EU grants only transition periods, but no permanent exemptions in fisheries, and refers to Malta’s experience.
detail.undanthagur.2: Albert Jónsson, former ambassador, points to what he sees as an incompatibility between Iceland’s non-negotiable demands for control over natural resources and the EU’s fundamental rules on integration. Ögmundur Jónasson says in Vikublaðið that temporary exemptions are not enough, and Erna Bjarnadóttir adds on Heimssýn that special arrangements are not legally permanent.
detail.evra.0: The NO side claims that the euro is no magic solution: growth in the euro area is far lower than in Iceland. It points out that Finland, which uses the euro, has the weakest growth in the Nordic countries and that the trade-off of the euro is lower growth and higher unemployment.
detail.evra.1: Lilja Dögg Alfreðsdóttir, deputy chair of Framsóknarflokkurinn, says that growth in the euro area is 1% versus 2,5% in Iceland, and that the trade-off of the euro is lower growth and higher unemployment. Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, former president, sets out economic arguments against membership on Heimssýn’s website and says that Iceland, Norway and Switzerland are growing faster than the EU states.
detail.evra.2: On Nútíminn, Ólafur Ragnar adds that no Nordic neighbouring country uses the euro except Finland and calls the EU debate ideological froth rather than facts. Einar Sigurðsson, chairman of the board of Ísfélagið, says in Eyjafréttir that Iceland is not ready for the euro and wants to postpone the vote while inflation is high.
detail.hervaeding.0: The NO side says that the EU merges the foreign and military policies of its member states and requires increased military spending. In its view, Iceland should remain a country without a military and a voice for peace outside the military alliances of great powers.
detail.hervaeding.1: Ágúst Valves Jóhannesson of Til vinstri við ESB writes that the EU is merging its foreign and military policy and that Iceland should remain a country without a military for the foreseeable future and stand with small nations. In a press release from the same organisation, Jökull Sólberg says that militarisation threatens Iceland’s role in peace and that the country should be an advocate for peace outside the EU. At the founding of the organisation, there was also a warning about the danger of Icelanders being drawn into EU militarisation.
detail.hervaeding.2: Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of Heimssýn, mentions militarisation among his arguments against membership in an article on DV. Guðmunda G. Guðmundsdóttir writes on Vísir that EU militarisation and the adoption of its foreign policy are causes for concern.
detail.ahrifaleysi.0: The NO side points out that Iceland would get about 6 seats out of 720 in the European Parliament and about 0,08% voting weight in the Council of Ministers. In its view, remote power in Brussels would be even more distant from rural areas than power in Reykjavík already is.
detail.ahrifaleysi.1: Hreinn Loftsson writes for Heimssýn that membership would mean only 6 seats out of 720, along with a weaker special position for Iceland in security matters. Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson says in Skessuhorn that Iceland’s weight would be about 0,08% when control rights over fishery resources were transferred to Brussels, and considers Ireland’s experience a warning.
detail.ahrifaleysi.2: In an article in Austurfrétt, the neglect of East Iceland by central power in the capital is linked to even more distant power in Brussels, and it is argued that ETS rules raise production costs in rural areas. Kjartan Magnússon of Ung gegn ESB says that a yes vote would amount to a mandate for an extensive adaptation process that would be difficult to reverse.
detail.kostnadur.0: The NO side says that membership would cost about 30 billion krónur a year in contributions and that the negotiations themselves cost about 2 billion. It also says that EU climate rules have already cost Iceland tens of billions.
detail.kostnadur.1: Hannes Hólmsteinn Gissurarson writes for Heimssýn that membership would cost about 30 billion annually. Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of Heimssýn, mentions in an article on DV a cost of more than 100 billion annually. Guðmunda G. Guðmundsdóttir says on Vísir that the negotiations would cost about 2 billion and the vote itself 600–700 million.
detail.kostnadur.2: On the website Frjálst land, it is claimed that participation in the EU emissions trading system cost Iceland 144 billion in the years 2017–2024. Hnikarr Bjarmi Franklínsson writes on Vísir that the process would take 3–4 years, tie up the administration and freeze other free-trade agreements. Hildur Sverrisdóttir, parliamentary group chair of Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn, calls the negotiations a waste of time and money.
detail.oafturkraeft.0: The NO side refers to the experience of Brexit and says it shows that leaving the EU is enormously difficult and costly. Membership is therefore, in practice, an irreversible commitment for a small state.
detail.oafturkraeft.1: Erlendur Magnússon writes on Vísir that EU membership is an almost irreversible commitment for a small state, as Brexit has shown. Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of Heimssýn, says in an article on DV that withdrawal is almost impossible and adds that no one applies for membership unless they want to join.
detail.oafturkraeft.2: Hannes Hólmsteinn Gissurarson argues on Heimssýn that the EU has evolved from a customs union into a centrally governed federal state — a development which the NO side believes would be difficult to undo after accession.
detail.landbunadur.0: The NO side says that accession would remove tariff protection and that domestic food production, especially dairy production, would then not withstand competition. In its view, promises of lower prices for consumers are greatly exaggerated.
detail.landbunadur.1: Herdís Magna Gunnarsdóttir, a dairy farmer, warns in Austurfrétt that dairy production would run into difficulties without tariff protection and doubts that food prices would fall significantly for consumers. Erna Bjarnadóttir writes in Eyjafréttir that claims of up to a 25% reduction in food prices do not hold up: the actual reduction is closer to 3%, and many goods are already duty-free. On BB.is she also points out that there are no examples of permanent exemptions from the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy.
detail.landbunadur.2: Margrét Ágústa Sigurðardóttir, managing director of Bændasamtakanna, criticizes in Bændablaðið that the parliamentary resolution contains no negotiating objectives and that, without an analysis of interests, the nation cannot take an informed position. Ögmundur Jónasson, former minister, points out in Vikublaðið that the agriculture chapter was never opened in the 2009–2013 talks and says temporary exemptions are not enough.
detail.nagrannar.0: The NO side points out that Norway, Switzerland, Greenland and the Faroe Islands all remain outside the EU and are doing well. In its view, Iceland has more in common with these neighboring nations than with the continent.
detail.nagrannar.1: Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, former president, sets out geographical and economic arguments against accession on Heimssýn’s website: no neighboring country is in the EU, and Iceland, Norway and Switzerland are growing faster than the EU states. On Nútímanum he adds that no Nordic neighboring nation uses the euro except Finland, and that the real-world examples do not fit the ideology of the EU.
detail.nagrannar.2: Hannes Hólmsteinn Gissurarson argues on Heimssýn that the EU has evolved from a customs union into a centrally governed federal state, and that membership would cost, among other things, independent trade agreements. Ingibjörg Isaksen writes in Vikublaðið that EU centralization is increasing and that control over fisheries and energy should remain at home.
motrok.vextir.0.title: Nothing about interest rates is negotiated in an accession treaty
motrok.vextir.0.text: Haraldur Ólafsson, chairman of Heimssýn, points out that no provision on the level of interest rates would be negotiated in an EU accession treaty; interest rates are determined by each country’s economic conditions and risk. He says lower interest rates are a prerequisite for being able to adopt the euro, not an automatic consequence of membership.
motrok.vextir.1.title: The euro’s trade-off: lower growth, higher unemployment
motrok.vextir.1.text: Lilja Dögg Alfreðsdóttir, deputy chair of Framsóknarflokkurinn, says in an article on Heimssýn’s website that eurozone growth is about 1%, compared with 2.5% in Iceland. The trade-off for the euro’s low interest rates is lower growth and higher unemployment than Icelanders have.
motrok.vextir.2.title: Finland with the euro — weakest economic growth in the Nordics
motrok.vextir.2.text: Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, former president, points out that Finland is the only Nordic neighboring country that uses the euro and also has the weakest economic growth in the Nordics; Iceland recovered faster from the financial crash than the EU states. The real-world examples do not match the promises made about the euro.
motrok.vextir.3.title: Iceland is not ready for the euro
motrok.vextir.3.text: Einar Sigurðsson, chairman of the board of Ísfélagið, says in Eyjafréttir that Iceland is not ready for the euro while inflation is high; the Maastricht criteria would first have to be met, and the fisheries sector needs stability in the meantime.
motrok.kikja.0.title: You cannot just take a look inside the package — alignment happens during the negotiations
motrok.kikja.0.text: Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson cites the EU’s own negotiating framework, which states that Iceland’s proper implementation and enforcement of the acquis will determine how quickly the negotiations proceed. Iceland would therefore in practice have to be fully aligned with the EU’s rules and administrative system by the time a possible treaty was on the table — this is not a matter of simply looking at the package, but of entering into it step by step.
motrok.kikja.1.title: The EU accepts applications for membership — not for talks
motrok.kikja.1.text: Economist Erna Bjarnadóttir points out that in 2009 Iceland formally applied for full membership under Article 49 of the EU Treaty. Talk of voting on “just talks” is misleading because the Union only accepts applications from states that want to join.
motrok.kikja.2.title: It is not possible to “resume” talks that broke off a decade ago
motrok.kikja.2.text: Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, said in his opinion on the parliamentary resolution that the question is misleading because it is not possible to resume talks that broke off more than a decade ago; less than a quarter of submissions supported the proposal unchanged. Heimssýn therefore says the question deserves a failing grade.
motrok.kikja.3.title: No one applies for membership unless they want to join
motrok.kikja.3.text: Haraldur Ólafsson, chairman of Heimssýn, responds that the vote is not a harmless expression of opinion: no one applies for EU membership unless they want to join the Union. The core issue is the surrender of sovereignty, the process is costly, and withdrawal is almost impossible once inside.
motrok.ahrif.0.title: 0.08% weight — equivalent to a 5% share in one MP
motrok.ahrif.0.text: Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson calls the seat at the table a myth: Iceland’s weight in the EU Council of Ministers would be about 0.08%, equivalent to a 5% share in one member of Alþingi, and in the European Parliament about 6 MEPs out of more than 700 — around 0.8%, corresponding to about half an MP. In the Commission, states in reality do not have representatives, since Commissioners are not permitted to favor their home country.
motrok.ahrif.1.title: Ireland’s experience: “We never had a chance"
motrok.ahrif.1.text: Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson points out that Ireland, with around five million inhabitants, was unable to prevent cuts to fishing quotas and the EU mackerel agreement despite having a seat at the table; leaders of Irish fishermen said they never had a chance. A seat at the table brings a small state painfully little real influence.
motrok.ahrif.2.title: 6 seats out of 720 instead of full control
motrok.ahrif.2.text: Hreinn Loftsson says in an article on Heimssýn’s website that instead of full control over fisheries and energy matters, Iceland would get only 6 seats out of 720 in the European Parliament; authority over the nation’s most important interests would shift to Brussels, where Iceland’s weight would be negligible.
motrok.kjor.0.title: The real reduction in food prices is close to 3%, not 25%
motrok.kjor.0.text: Economist Erna Bjarnadóttir rebuts claims of up to a 25% reduction in food prices with a concrete example: in a 2,590 krónur chicken wrap, the meat accounts for about 280–290 krónur, so a 25% reduction in meat prices would produce just under a 3% reduction in the price of the product. In addition, many products are already tariff-free from the EU under agreements from 2018, and products with active tariff protection account for only about 5.4% of household spending.
motrok.kjor.1.title: The price difference is explained by wages and transport costs, not the EU
motrok.kjor.1.text: Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of Heimssýn, says that when promises of cheaper food are examined more closely, the price difference turns out to be negligible — in the example of a chicken meal only about 65 krónur, not hundreds or thousands. He says the higher price level in Iceland is due to higher wages, transport costs, and the inefficiency of small scale, not to remaining outside the EU.
motrok.kjor.2.title: Dairy farmer: lower consumer prices unlikely, production at risk
motrok.kjor.2.text: Herdís Magna Gunnarsdóttir, a dairy farmer, says irresponsible claims are being made about agriculture and food prices: without tariff protection, domestic milk production would run into difficulties, while it is uncertain whether any reduction would be passed on to consumers to any significant extent.
motrok.kjor.3.title: Living standards are already better in Iceland than in EU countries
motrok.kjor.3.text: A report by Áfram Ísland compares living standards: Iceland ranks ahead of EU countries in economic growth, employment, productivity, purchasing power, and the state of public finances. The organisation therefore says that joining the Union would bring no improvement in living standards.
motrok.hraedslu.0.title: No is a legitimate position, not hostility to information
motrok.hraedslu.0.text: Erna Bjarnadóttir says the YES side is trying to shift the debate away from the substantive issues and onto whether people are „open or closed". NO is a legitimate democratic position, she says, not a lack of willingness to know more, since accession talks are not neutral information-gathering but a process with its own momentum, its own framework, and its own consequences.
motrok.hraedslu.1.title: The criticism is based on the EU’s own documents
motrok.hraedslu.1.text: Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson responds to talk of scaremongering by quoting directly from the EU’s negotiating framework: there the Union itself says that implementation of the acquis during the negotiations determines their pace. Warnings about adaptation are therefore documented in EU materials, not figments of the opponents’ imagination.
motrok.hraedslu.2.title: A NO vote is a critical assessment, not fear
motrok.hraedslu.2.text: Hnikarr Bjarmi Franklínsson says the YES side has presented the talks as an innocent and cost-free process. The NO position, however, is based on a critical assessment: the process would take 3–4 years, tie up the public administration, freeze other free-trade agreements, and cost money — weighing such costs is not fear.
motrok.hraedslu.3.title: Former ambassador points to a real incompatibility
motrok.hraedslu.3.text: Albert Jónsson, a former ambassador, points to an incompatibility between Iceland’s non-negotiable demands for control over its resources and the EU’s fundamental rules on integration. Concerns about sovereignty over resources are thus based on an analysis of the Union’s regulatory framework, not fearmongering.
motrok.serlausnir.0.title: Permanent exemptions were never on offer in 2009–2013
motrok.serlausnir.0.text: Hreinn Loftsson explains that EU representatives said from the outset of the 2009–2013 negotiations that no permanent exemption from the Union’s regulatory framework was on offer; the EU negotiating framework specified that exemptions would have to be temporary and limited in scope. He cites an analysis by law professor Stefán Már Stefánsson that no country has received a permanent exemption from the Common Fisheries Policy, since that would require a treaty change with the approval of all member states.
motrok.serlausnir.1.title: The quota would remain, but control rights would pass to Brussels
motrok.serlausnir.1.text: Hjörtur J. Guðmundsson responds directly to the claim that catch history would secure an Icelandic quota: although Icelanders would continue to own the resource, the right of control — the power to decide how it is used — would pass to Brussels, where Iceland’s weight would be about 0.08%. EU rules would govern the use of the resource even if ownership remained Icelandic.
motrok.serlausnir.2.title: Special arrangements are not exemptions
motrok.serlausnir.2.text: Erna Bjarnadóttir points out that there are no examples of permanent exemptions from the EU’s agricultural policy; what are called special arrangements, such as the Finns’ northern support, were built into the Union’s regulatory framework and subject to it — not an exemption from the policy itself.
motrok.serlausnir.3.title: Malta’s experience: transition periods, not permanent special status
motrok.serlausnir.3.text: Ágúst Valves Jóhannesson of Til vinstri við ESB says Malta’s experience shows that the EU grants only temporary transition periods in fisheries, not permanent exemptions; Malta’s special arrangements fall within the common policy and are subject to the authority of the European Commission.
motrok.oryggi.0.title: Iceland’s special position in NATO and the defence agreement with the United States guarantee security — not the EU
motrok.oryggi.0.text: Hreinn Loftsson writes on the Heimssýn website that Iceland’s special position as an unarmed nation within NATO, with a bilateral defence agreement with the United States, has ensured the country stability and peace; the EU has no military capabilities, and no member state of the Union has a comparable defence agreement. Membership could undermine the defence relationship with the United States and weaken Iceland’s special position in security affairs.
motrok.oryggi.1.title: Uncertainty over whether defence cooperation with the United States is compatible with the EU’s defence framework
motrok.oryggi.1.text: Björn Bjarnason, former minister, says that because of the government’s plans, new questions arise about how Iceland’s bilateral defence cooperation with the United States would be compatible with Iceland becoming part of the European Union’s security and defence framework, and calls for clear answers from the authorities on whether ties with the United States would change upon accession.
motrok.oryggi.2.title: Is the defence agreement being put at risk by EU talks?
motrok.oryggi.2.text: Stefán Vagn Stefánsson, chair of the parliamentary group of Framsóknarflokkurinn, pointed out in Alþingi that Iceland’s bilateral defence agreement with the United States was a unique arrangement among NATO states and asked whether the agreement was being put at risk by EU talks.
motrok.oryggi.3.title: The shelter is a militarised great-power alliance — Iceland should stay outside the disputes of the great powers
motrok.oryggi.3.text: Ágúst Valves Jóhannesson of Til vinstri við ESB says that the European Union is gradually uniting under a single foreign policy alongside defence matters; Iceland should remain a demilitarised country for the foreseeable future, free from all the disputes of the great powers, and its security does not lie in association with a larger power.
motrok.gildi.0.title: A democratic deficit characterizes the EU itself
motrok.gildi.0.text: In his book on the EU, Frosti Sigurjónsson argues that a democratic deficit characterizes the Union itself; power rests with institutions in which voters have little direct say, and the Union also faces ageing populations, unfunded pension systems, and debt.
motrok.gildi.1.title: Member of the European Parliament says the EU itself tries to influence other countries’ elections
motrok.gildi.1.text: MEP Fidias Panayiotou claims that the EU itself violates the democratic values it says it stands for: “We are trying to interfere in the elections in Moldova.” The remarks raise doubts about whether the Union lives up to its democratic promises.
motrok.gildi.2.title: Peace, democracy and humanitarianism are better served on our own terms outside the EU
motrok.gildi.2.text: Jökull Sólberg and Til vinstri við ESB say that Iceland should reject EU centralization and choose international cooperation on its own terms in the interests of peace, democracy and humanitarianism; the Union’s militarization threatens Iceland’s role for peace, and the group describes itself as pro-European while nevertheless rejecting membership.
motrok.lydraedi.0.title: The question is misleading, so the vote is not an informed democratic choice
motrok.lydraedi.0.text: Birgir Ármannsson, former Speaker of Alþingi, considers the question fundamentally misleading: it conflates the continuation of old talks with entirely new accession negotiations, meaning voters do not know exactly what they are voting on.
motrok.lydraedi.1.title: Baudenbacher: it is not possible to “continue” talks that broke off a decade ago
motrok.lydraedi.1.text: Heimssýn points out that fewer than a quarter of the submissions on the parliamentary resolution supported it unchanged, and that Carl Baudenbacher, former President of the EFTA Court, considered the question misleading because it is not possible to continue talks that broke off a decade ago.
motrok.lydraedi.2.title: An advisory vote with low turnout provides a weak mandate
motrok.lydraedi.2.text: Páll Vilhjálmsson says that since the vote would only be advisory, it invites disputes over interpretation: if turnout were close to 50% and yes won by a narrow majority, the authorities would be basing the talks on the support of a minority of eligible voters — far too weak a mandate for such major changes.
motrok.lydraedi.3.title: No is also a democratic position
motrok.lydraedi.3.text: Erna Bjarnadóttir says that no is a legitimate democratic position that is wrongly dismissed as hostility to information; accession talks are not a neutral fact-finding exercise, and the democratic argument of the YES side assumes that only one answer is “informed”.
motrok.byggd.0.title: Iceland would pay more into EU funds than it would get back
motrok.byggd.0.text: Haraldur Ólafsson, chair of Heimssýn, says that the amounts Iceland might receive from individual funds would be only a small fraction of the contributions the country would have to pay; the EU’s cohesion and regional development funds are intended primarily for poorer states in Southern and Eastern Europe, whereas Iceland is one of the more affluent countries on the continent and would be a net contributor.
motrok.byggd.1.title: Brussels would be an even more distant authority for rural Iceland than Reykjavík
motrok.byggd.1.text: In a submitted opinion piece in Austurfrétt, it is questioned whether EU funding would improve the position of rural Iceland: it asks whether its voice would carry more weight, points out that EU rules such as the ETS emissions trading system, “thoughtlessly incorporated into Icelandic law in 2007”, raise the price of all inputs and production and reduce people’s purchasing power — remote power in Brussels would not remedy the neglect of the authorities in Reykjavík.
motrok.taekifaeri.0.title: The euro is not the solution for young people — an independent currency suits a volatile economy
motrok.taekifaeri.0.text: Kjartan Magnússon, a board member of Ung gegn ESB, acknowledges that high interest rates have led many people, especially young people, to look to the euro as a possible solution, but says an independent currency is the better option because the Icelandic economy is based on volatile industries; Iceland recovered more quickly from economic crisis than the eurozone countries Greece and Spain.
motrok.taekifaeri.1.title: Membership binds future generations to an almost irreversible commitment
motrok.taekifaeri.1.text: Erlendur Magnússon says that the experience of the United Kingdom shows that leaving the EU is “almost impossible” and, for a small country like Iceland, “virtually impossible”; the current generation cannot allow itself “to bind our descendants in the shackles of the European Union for ever and ever” — the opportunity for young people lies in keeping the options open.
motrok.taekifaeri.2.title: Housing problems and youth unemployment are worse within the EU
motrok.taekifaeri.2.text: An article on BB.is points out that young people’s housing difficulties are severe in many parts of the EU despite low interest rates: in many European countries, young people find it harder to buy housing, high rents create rental poverty traps, and youth unemployment within the EU has historically been much higher than in Iceland.
motrok.fullveldi.0.title: Sovereignty lies in the right to negotiate
motrok.fullveldi.0.text: Helga Vala Helgadóttir says that sovereignty lies precisely in a state’s ability to conclude international agreements — sovereign states have always entered into such agreements — and criticizes attempts to stir up fear that Iceland’s sovereignty is at risk merely by entering into negotiations; in any case, the nation will have the final say on the agreement.
motrok.fullveldi.1.title: The EEA arrangement is unbecoming of a sovereign state
motrok.fullveldi.1.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon, chair of Evrópuhreyfingin, points out that Iceland already adopts 75–80% of the EU’s internal market rules through the EEA — “rules that we have had no part in making at any stage of the process” — and says that real power over its own regulatory framework comes precisely through membership, not by maintaining the status quo.
motrok.fullveldi.2.title: A right to shape, but no right to decide, today
motrok.fullveldi.2.text: Kristján Vigfússon explains that the EEA states have only a limited right to shape EU legislation at the preparatory stage, but no right to decide — at the drafting and adoption stages they have no formal involvement — and asks whether that arrangement is acceptable for a sovereign nation.
motrok.fullveldi.3.title: Sovereignty lies in an informed choice
motrok.fullveldi.3.text: Jóhannes Finnur Halldórsson writes that Iceland is already in the EEA and Schengen without full influence, and that sovereignty lies in the nation making an informed decision itself — negotiations are a natural continuation of the European cooperation already in place, not a departure from sovereignty.
motrok.sjavarutvegur.0.title: Fishing track record decides — the quota would remain Icelandic
motrok.sjavarutvegur.0.text: Thomas Möller, a board member of Evrópuhreyfingin, points out that fishing rights within the EU are based on historical use (relative stability); no other nations have a fishing track record for the main demersal fish stocks in Icelandic waters, and the quota would therefore continue to belong to Icelanders.
motrok.sjavarutvegur.1.title: Malta obtained special arrangements in fisheries
motrok.sjavarutvegur.1.text: Pawel Bartoszek, chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee, points out that “Malta did in fact get fairly extensive special arrangements in its accession treaty … in the field of fisheries” and that fisheries and agriculture are matters for negotiation — the experience of small states shows that they can be negotiated.
motrok.sjavarutvegur.2.title: Full control over marine resources is a red line
motrok.sjavarutvegur.2.text: Þórður Snær Júlíusson explains that Iceland’s negotiating objectives, according to the opinion of the majority of the Foreign Affairs Committee, stipulate “full control over marine resources, fisheries management, and the sustainable use of fish stocks” — control over the nation’s key resources is defined as a red line in the negotiations.
motrok.spurning.0.title: The question is about negotiations, not accession
motrok.spurning.0.text: Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says: “The question here is not whether the nation should join, but whether we should enter into negotiations” — a decision on membership will not be taken until the nation has seen a completed agreement and voted on it separately in a second referendum.
motrok.spurning.1.title: The Venice Commission confirms the nature of the vote
motrok.spurning.1.text: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson points out that the Venice Commission has confirmed that a yes vote does not automatically lead to EU membership, but only to the opening of accession talks, and that the Commission reiterates that a second referendum on actual membership will be held once negotiations are concluded.
motrok.spurning.2.title: Membership is not on the table
motrok.spurning.2.text: Pawel Bartoszek says the no movement is misleadingly equating negotiations with membership: “Iceland’s membership of the European Union is not on the table” — membership would require negotiations, a completed agreement, the approval of all member states, and a second referendum.
motrok.adlogun.0.title: No adaptation took place in 2009–2013
motrok.adlogun.0.text: Halldór Jörgen Olesen rejects the adaptation arguments by referring to experience: during the 2009–2013 talks, no adaptation took place — neither legislative changes nor institutional changes — as confirmed by the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in May 2026; EU IPA grants went to projects such as ecosystem mapping and translations of the regulatory framework. “A yes is not a yes to the EU. A yes is a yes to negotiate.”
motrok.adlogun.1.title: No systemic changes without a second vote
motrok.adlogun.1.text: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says that nothing in Iceland’s system of government will be changed on the basis of the negotiations themselves; the government will sit at the table with clear negotiating objectives, and no changes will take effect until the nation has approved a completed agreement in a second referendum.
motrok.adlogun.2.title: A yes vote only opens the negotiation process
motrok.adlogun.2.text: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson refers to the Venice Commission’s opinion that a yes vote leads only to the opening of the negotiation process — neither to membership nor to irreversible changes — and that the authorities must ensure that the final decision is taken in a separate vote on the agreement itself.
motrok.ees.0.title: 75–80% of rules implemented without any influence
motrok.ees.0.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon says that Iceland already implements 75–80% of EU internal market legislation through the EEA without having had any say at any stage in drafting those rules — so the EEA only "works" by giving up the influence that full membership would provide.
motrok.ees.1.title: The formal influence of EEA states ends at the preparatory stage
motrok.ees.1.text: Kristján Vigfússon outlines the EU legislative process in three stages and shows that the formal influence of the EEA states already ends at the preparatory stage; at the processing and adoption stages they have no involvement, and with the increased power of the European Parliament the involvement of the EEA states has "become more complex and weakened somewhat".
motrok.ees.2.title: The EEA was a temporary solution
motrok.ees.2.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson, a former minister, says that "the supplementary membership through the EEA was a temporary solution" — an excellent outcome at the time, but "not a permanent solution and democratically unacceptable in the long run"; the logical next step is to conclude the negotiations and vote on a completed agreement.
motrok.ees.3.title: Today the voting weight is zero
motrok.ees.3.text: Hjálmar Vilhjálmsson, a board member of SJÁ, calculates using the Banzhaf method that each Icelander’s voting weight in the EU Council of Ministers would be about 37 times that of each German — but in the current EEA arrangement the weight of Icelanders in decisions on the rules they now implement is zero.
motrok.efnahagur.0.title: The image of a stagnant EU is outdated
motrok.efnahagur.0.text: Thomas Möller says opponents rely on an outdated image of Europe: the EU economy grew by 14% in 2008–2023 and is the world’s second-largest economy, euro area growth (1.5%) compares well with the United States, and about 3.5 million companies were established in EU countries in 2023, most of them innovative firms.
motrok.efnahagur.1.title: The hidden cost of the króna is overlooked in the comparison
motrok.efnahagur.1.text: Óðinn Freyr Baldursson points out that Iceland’s success outside the EU carries hidden costs: around 1.000 billion krónur, about 20% of GDP, are tied up in foreign exchange reserves, and Icelandic households and businesses pay more than 100 billion a year in interest costs due to the instability of the króna — a cost that falls heaviest on those least able to bear it.
motrok.efnahagur.2.title: The króna costs around 300 billion a year
motrok.efnahagur.2.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson estimates that an independent floating króna costs “a conservatively estimated 300 billion a year, divided equally among households, businesses and the public sector” and says the current currency system is “fully exhausted” — meaning that prosperity outside the EU comes at a higher price than the comparison figures cited by the NO side suggest.
motrok.umbod.0.title: The referendum itself is the search for a mandate
motrok.umbod.0.text: Helga Vala Helgadóttir responds to criticism about a lack of mandate by arguing that parliamentary elections are never about one single issue; a referendum is precisely the right tool for seeking a clear mandate from the nation on major issues between parliamentary elections — democracy is about giving the nation the opportunity to express itself now, not only once every four years.
motrok.umbod.1.title: No blank cheque — the objectives are already clear
motrok.umbod.1.text: Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says the government is not being given a blank cheque: the negotiating objectives are set out in the opinion of the majority on the Foreign Affairs Committee, with precise conditions regarding fisheries, agriculture and energy, and the nation will have the final say on the outcome in a second vote.
motrok.umbod.2.title: The negotiating objectives have been public since 18 May
motrok.umbod.2.text: Þórður Snær Júlíusson responds to claims that no negotiating objectives exist: they have been publicly available since 18. maí 2026 in the opinion of the majority on the Foreign Affairs Committee, with defined red lines on marine resources, water, energy and agriculture.
motrok.umbod.3.title: A dual democratic process
motrok.umbod.3.text: Ingibjörg Sólrún Gísladóttir, former Minister for Foreign Affairs, says the core of the issue is a dual democratic process: the nation first votes on whether talks should continue and later votes again on the agreement itself — it would be hard to find a stronger democratic mandate for the process.
motrok.undanthagur.0.title: Sweden, Finland and Malta secured special arrangements
motrok.undanthagur.0.text: Pawel Bartoszek notes that Sweden and Finland secured special arrangements in their accession treaties and that Malta obtained “quite extensive special solutions … in the field of fisheries” — experience shows that special solutions for small states are a real part of accession treaties, not wishful thinking.
motrok.undanthagur.1.title: All new member states received agreements tailored to their particular circumstances
motrok.undanthagur.1.text: Thomas Möller claims that the accession treaties of all new member states in recent decades were adapted to each country’s particular circumstances through special provisions, and that Iceland’s negotiating position has improved significantly — Iceland would bring the EU, among other things, about 700 thousand square kilometres of maritime area and a key strategic position in North Atlantic security matters.
motrok.undanthagur.2.title: Special arrangements are the rule, not the exception
motrok.undanthagur.2.text: Thomas Möller argues that special arrangements are “the rule rather than the exception” within the EU, and that the Union has a strong history of tailoring accession treaties to the particular circumstances of island states; moreover, the allocation of fishing rights is based on historical use, which would safeguard Icelandic interests regardless of the wording on permanence.
motrok.evra.0.title: The króna has costs of its own
motrok.evra.0.text: Óðinn Freyr Baldursson points out that maintaining the króna comes at enormous cost: about 1.000 billion krónur, around 20% of GDP, are tied up in foreign exchange reserves; households and businesses pay over 100 billion a year in interest costs because of the króna’s instability and less favourable borrowing terms; and currency exchange cost about 12,4 billion in 2025. The króna also amplifies economic shocks and deters foreign investment.
motrok.evra.1.title: The króna costs around 300 billion a year
motrok.evra.1.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson estimates the cost of an independent, floating króna at “a conservatively estimated 300 billion a year, divided equally between households, businesses and the public sector in the form of interest-rate differentials”, and says the current monetary arrangement has been “fully tested” — membership of the monetary union is the most important of the benefits of full membership.
motrok.evra.2.title: The growth comparison is misleading per person
motrok.evra.2.text: Sveinn Agnarsson, professor of economics at HÍ, points out that although total economic growth in 2014–2025 was 2.8% in Iceland compared with 1.5% in the euro area, the picture reverses when looking at GDP per capita: 1.0% annual growth in Iceland versus 1.2% in the euro area — and fluctuations in growth are also much greater in Iceland (standard deviation 4.0 versus 2.8).
motrok.evra.3.title: Usurious interest rates have accompanied the króna for more than a century
motrok.evra.3.text: Dóra Magnúsdóttir says the public and small businesses pay much higher interest rates than comparable nations, and that the interest burden has plagued Icelanders for more than a full century; the euro is the only realistic tool for escaping “interest-rate servitude” — large companies already settle in euros, while small family businesses and households are left behind with króna interest rates.
motrok.hervaeding.0.title: There is no European army — and Iceland would have a veto
motrok.hervaeding.0.text: Óðinn Freyr Baldursson points out that no European army exists; the idea is “the brainchild of one man” rather than EU policy. The creation of a joint military force would require the unanimous approval of all member states, so Iceland alone could block it; defence and security matters remain under the authority of each state under the Lisbon Treaty. Iceland has been without an army within NATO since 1949, without pressure to create one — why should an economic union require what the world’s largest military alliance never did?
motrok.hervaeding.1.title: Similar dire predictions have proved wrong before
motrok.hervaeding.1.text: Guðfinna Jóh. Guðmundsdóttir says claims about militarisation and loss of sovereignty are part of fearmongering against the talks; earlier dire predictions about NATO, EFTA and the EEA all proved wrong, and it is more sensible to see the agreement before passing judgment.
motrok.ahrifaleysi.0.title: Each Icelander’s voting weight would be 37 times that of a German
motrok.ahrifaleysi.0.text: Using the Banzhaf power index, Hjálmar Vilhjálmsson calculates that Germany’s decisive voting weight in the Council of Ministers would be only just under six times that of Iceland, even though Germans are about 209 times more numerous — each Icelander would have about 37 times the weight of each German, equivalent to roughly 15 million Germans. Qualified majority voting (QMV) requires the support of at least 55% of member states and 65% of the population, which ensures weight for small states — and today Iceland’s voting weight is zero.
motrok.ahrifaleysi.1.title: The smallest nations have proportionally the most weight — and are the most satisfied
motrok.ahrifaleysi.1.text: Páll Rafnar Þorsteinsson points out that, relative to population, the smallest nations have many times more representatives than the largest; in addition to parliamentary seats, Iceland would receive a full seat in the Council of Ministers, a commissioner and a judge. Small states measure as the most satisfied with membership in Eurobarometer: Ireland 93%, Luxembourg and Malta 91%. Concerns about lack of influence are "entirely a home-made inferiority complex".
motrok.ahrifaleysi.2.title: Six parliamentary seats are more than the EEA’s zero influence
motrok.ahrifaleysi.2.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon points out that Iceland already adopts 75–80% of EU internal market rules through the EEA without any voting rights; the current situation is unworthy of a sovereign state, and full membership would provide real power instead of today’s complete lack of influence.
motrok.kostnadur.0.title: Membership fees are outweighed by savings in the tens or hundreds of billions
motrok.kostnadur.0.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon acknowledges that direct membership fees would increase, but says that extra cost would quickly be offset by savings that would "run to tens, even hundreds of billions per year" from eliminating the costs of maintaining foreign exchange reserves, tariffs and the krona’s excessive interest rates. In addition, EU regional development funds spend each year about five times more than the entire Icelandic state budget allocates to such projects.
motrok.kostnadur.1.title: Net contribution would be closer to 2–7 billion than 30
motrok.kostnadur.1.text: According to the information website jaedanei.is, Iceland’s annual net contribution after accession would be around 2–7 billion krónur per year (about 0.2–0.3% of GDP based on the Finnish precedent), since the EEA contributions, about 8 billion per year, would cease — and in addition the roughly 1.4 billion in annual tariffs on seafood products to the EU would disappear within the customs union.
motrok.kostnadur.2.title: The króna costs many times more than membership
motrok.kostnadur.2.text: Björgvin G. Sigurðsson says the cost to the national economy of an independent, floating króna is conservatively estimated at around 300 billion a year in the form of an interest-rate differential, divided equally between households, businesses and the public sector — an amount on an entirely different scale from the membership contributions under discussion.
motrok.oafturkraeft.0.title: A YES vote only opens the negotiating table — nothing is settled
motrok.oafturkraeft.0.text: Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir says: “If the result is yes, the door to the negotiating table opens. Nothing else.” Nothing is settled until the process is complete “and then only if the nation itself approves the outcome” in a second referendum on a fully negotiated agreement.
motrok.oafturkraeft.1.title: No legislative changes occurred during the 2009–2013 talks
motrok.oafturkraeft.1.text: Halldór Jörgen Olesen points out that no legislative changes took place during the 2009–2013 negotiation period, and that the Ministry for Foreign Affairs confirmed that no adaptation took place beyond the ordinary obligations of the EEA. A YES vote “opens negotiations. Nothing else” — the nation “keeps all its cards in hand and gets another chance to say no if the agreement is not suitable.”
motrok.oafturkraeft.2.title: Article 50 is a formal exit procedure — Brexit proves that leaving is possible
motrok.oafturkraeft.2.text: According to the information website jaedanei.is, withdrawal from the EU is formally guaranteed in Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon — the same process the British used for Brexit — so membership is not irreversible. Before membership could happen, in addition to a second referendum, a constitutional amendment would be required, which two parliaments would have to approve with an election in between.
motrok.landbunadur.0.title: Negotiating objectives: food security, regional settlement and a ban on imports of live animals
motrok.landbunadur.0.text: Þórður Snær Júlíusson says that Iceland would fight for special arrangements in agriculture because of more difficult production conditions: “Production conditions in Iceland are more difficult than in most of Europe. That is why support must ensure food security, regional settlement and continued farming.” The ban on imports of live animals must also remain in place to protect Icelandic livestock breeds.
motrok.landbunadur.1.title: Sweden and Finland secured special arrangements in agriculture
motrok.landbunadur.1.text: Pawel Bartoszek points out that Sweden and Finland obtained a special arrangement in agriculture (northern aid) when they joined the EU, and that Malta received “rather extensive special arrangements in its accession treaty” that still apply — there are therefore precedents for special arrangements for agriculture in northern regions.
motrok.landbunadur.2.title: Opportunities for Icelandic products in larger markets
motrok.landbunadur.2.text: Magnús Árni Skjöld Magnússon says that Icelandic farmers could make use of their distinctive position and expand into larger markets with Icelandic products; he asks whether the state of agriculture is really so good “that it would not be worthwhile for farmers to find out whether there might be, even considerable, opportunities for strengthening it” in negotiations.
motrok.landbunadur.3.title: Food prices could fall by 25–30%
motrok.landbunadur.3.text: Thomas Möller argues, against claims that price reductions are exaggerated, that food prices could fall by 25–30% with membership and interest rates drop from about 9% to about 3%; a NO vote would close the door on these terms for generations.
motrok.nagrannar.0.title: Seven EU states among the top 15 — Norway’s and Switzerland’s prosperity has other explanations
motrok.nagrannar.0.text: Political scientist Elvar Örn Arason points out that seven EU states rank among the top 15 countries on the United Nations standard-of-living index: Denmark, Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland and Finland. The position of Norway and Switzerland is explained by “the exceptional resource wealth of one and the other’s special role as a financial centre — not by their being outside the EU”. Iceland and Norway base their prosperity on close ties to the internal market and are “almost associate members of the Union” without a seat at the table where the legislation is drafted.
motrok.nagrannar.1.title: Most of the old EFTA states joined and are well satisfied with their lot
motrok.nagrannar.1.text: Ingibjörg Sólrún Gísladóttir points out that “most of the states that belonged to EFTA when Iceland became a member have become full members of the EU” and are well satisfied with their situation within the Union; in a more dangerous world, it is important to have friends and allies who can come to one’s aid.
